title: The Reading Machine and the Date: Queens, Cambridge, and the Argument Against Dying

segments.name: Queens: The Refugee House and the Machine That Composed

stops.name: Queens, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. English Wikipedia gives 12 February 1948, Queens, New York City, and names the parents as Fredric Kurzweil, pianist and conductor, and Hannah Kurzweil, visual artist, Austrian Jewish refugees. No source reached names the hospital or the neighbourhood, so the coordinate is a general borough point rather than a located address. The P.S. 188 attendance is named by Wikipedia without a street address and is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Fredric Kurzweil, pianist and conductor, and Hannah Kurzweil, a visual artist, are Austrian Jews who got out; their son is born in Queens on the twelfth of February. No source reached names the hospital, so the pin marks the borough and nothing finer. The house is musical and short of money, an emigre household in a borough full of them, and the boy grows up among salvaged parts and the assumption that a machine is a thing you take apart to see how it works. He goes on to P.S. 188, the Kingsbury School, a few streets away.
suggested_refs: P.S. 188, the Kingsbury School, Queens

stops.name: Queens Village, Martin Van Buren High School
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was Martin Van Buren High School class of 1965 and that the school stands at 230-17 Hillside Avenue, Queens Village; the coordinate 40.7333, -73.7392 is Wikipedia's for the school and corrects a figure roughly 1.3 kilometres south that circulates in the research pool. The 1961 entry year is inferred from the class year and the month defaults to the start of the school year. The claim that this school produced more Westinghouse Science Talent Search winners than any other in the country appears in no source that could be checked and is not asserted.
stops.campa: He enters Martin Van Buren High School on Hillside Avenue in Queens Village, class of 1965. At about fifteen he writes a program that reads the works of classical composers, extracts the statistical regularities in their part-writing, and generates new melodies by the same rules. It runs on borrowed machine time and it works well enough to be played aloud to strangers. The flourish that circulates later, that this school sent more Westinghouse winners to the finals than any other in the country, appears in nothing that could be checked.
suggested_refs: Martin Van Buren High School, 230-17 Hillside Avenue, Queens Village
sources: Academy of Achievement, 'Ray Kurzweil' interview, achievement.org

stops.name: Cambridge, the letter to Minsky
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, reconstructed as to date and room. The Academy of Achievement interview has him communicating with Marvin Minsky while in high school and visiting him in Boston; no source reached gives a date or a building, so the year orders the segment and the pin is the canonical MIT coordinate. The parallel claim that he also visited Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell circulates widely in profiles of him but was found in neither Wikipedia nor the Academy of Achievement transcript, and is carried as unverified rather than staged as a stop.
stops.campa: Still in high school, he writes to Marvin Minsky at MIT. Minsky writes back, then asks him to come up to Boston, and they spend a day talking. Minsky is at that moment the loudest advocate of the symbolic approach to machine intelligence and a few years from the book that will bury neural networks for a decade and a half. No source reached gives the date or the room. What Kurzweil keeps of the day, telling it decades later, is that the man treated a schoolboy exactly as he would have treated a professor.
suggested_refs: The Academy of Achievement interview with Kurzweil, in which he describes the Minsky visit
sources: Academy of Achievement, 'Ray Kurzweil' interview, achievement.org

stops.name: New York, I've Got a Secret
stops.date_confidence: attested that the appearance happened and that he demonstrated computer-composed music on the CBS panel show; the sources disagree about the year, Wikipedia placing it in 1965 while the Academy of Achievement transcript gives his age as sixteen, which back-calculates to 1964. The contradiction is recorded rather than resolved. The studio address is documented nowhere reached and the coordinate is a general midtown Manhattan point. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: A teenager walks onto the set of a CBS panel show carrying a secret the audience is told and the panel is not: the piano piece he is about to play was written by a computer he built himself. The program reads the note-by-note habits of classical composers and produces new music in their manner. What the stunt takes for granted is that a mind's output can be analysed into patterns and the patterns run forward. He is not yet in college. Wikipedia dates the appearance to 1965; the Academy of Achievement transcript has him sixteen, which puts it in 1964.
suggested_refs: Surviving kinescopes of the CBS panel show I've Got a Secret from the 1964-1965 seasons
sources: Academy of Achievement, 'Ray Kurzweil' interview, achievement.org

stops.name: MIT, the freshman who has already finished
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied at MIT and graduated in 1970 with a B.S. in computer science and literature. The claim that he worked through the entire programming curriculum in about a year and a half is his own retrospective account and is not independently documented. September 1965 is the ordinary start of the academic year and orders the segment.
stops.campa: He enrols at MIT to study with Minsky, and finds, by his own later account, that he has worked through everything the programming curriculum has to offer in about a year and a half. Nobody else documents this. So he takes literature alongside computer science and starts companies in the gaps. He will hold longer than most of the people who taught it to him the bet the Institute is making in these years: intelligence as the manipulation of tokens by rules, the mind as a program that can in principle be written out.

stops.name: New York, the program sold to Harcourt
stops.date_confidence: attested through Wikipedia that in his sophomore year he devised the Select College Consulting Program and sold it to Harcourt, Brace and World for a reported hundred thousand dollars plus royalties. stops.campa: In his sophomore year he builds the Select College Consulting Program: a database of some three thousand colleges, roughly two million facts, and a rule system that turns a student's answers into a shortlist. It is an expert system before the phrase is in circulation, and he sells it to the publisher Harcourt, Brace and World for a reported hundred thousand dollars plus royalties. He is twenty. The publisher's address is in no source reached, so the pin sits in the midtown publishing district generally.
suggested_refs: Harcourt, Brace and World's Select College Consulting Program materials, late 1960s

stops.name: Queens, the death of Fredric Kurzweil
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact through the American Foundation for the Blind oral history of 12 November 2004, in which Kurzweil says his father died when he was twenty-two and his father was fifty-eight, and confirms heart disease. Note that Wikipedia's article on him carries nothing about the death, so the attribution to Wikipedia found in the research pool is wrong. The city and the hospital are undocumented and the coordinate is a placeholder near the family's New York base. Since he turned twenty-two on 12 February 1970, the death falls after that date; month and day default to 01 because nothing narrows it.
stops.campa: Fredric Kurzweil dies of heart disease at fifty-eight. His son is twenty-two. In the oral history he records thirty-four years later he gives the two numbers exactly that way, one after the other: a father whose heart failed early, a son who intends not to repeat it. Where the death occurred is recorded in nothing reachable, and Wikipedia's article on him carries nothing about it at all. He keeps his father's papers, some fifty boxes of letters and scores and photographs, and throws none of it out.
suggested_refs: The fifty boxes of Fredric Kurzweil's papers, letters, scores and photographs, retained by his son since 1970
Amy Kurzweil, Artificial: A Love Story (Catapult, 17 October 2023), the granddaughter's account of the same archive
sources: American Foundation for the Blind, 'Interviews with Technology Pioneers: Ray Kurzweil', 12 November 2004, afb.org

stops.name: MIT, the degree in computer science and literature
stops.date_confidence: attested that he graduated from MIT in 1970 with a B.S. in computer science and literature; the month of the commencement is not stated in any source reached and June is the Institute's ordinary date, used to order the segment.
stops.campa: He takes the bachelor's degree in computer science and literature. The double field holds for the next half-century: machines that handle text, books that argue about the future in a novelist's register of dates and scenes. The month of the commencement is stated in nothing reached, and June is the Institute's ordinary date. He is already a man who has sold a company, and he leaves Cambridge for the first venture to carry his own name on the door. The year the diploma is issued is the year his father dies.

stops.name: Cambridge, Kurzweil Computer Products
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: Wikipedia's articles on Kurzweil, on optical character recognition, and on the Nuance corporate lineage all give 1974, correcting the '1973/1974' hedge in the research pool. No source reached gives the company's street address, so the coordinate is a general Cambridge placeholder up near Porter Square and should not be read as a located site. The priority claim is contested: Wikipedia's OCR article notes that omni-font recognition 'was already in use by other companies like CompuScan during the late 1960s and 1970s.' Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He founds Kurzweil Computer Products to solve a problem nobody has solved: reading. The optical character recognition that exists works only on a specific typeface printed to specification. He wants omni-font, a machine that takes any printed page and returns the letters. The company builds one, along with a charge-coupled flatbed scanner and a text-to-speech synthesizer, three inventions that only matter when they are in the same box. Priority is contested; CompuScan and others were working the same ground through the late sixties.
suggested_refs: The charge-coupled device flatbed scanner developed at Kurzweil Computer Products, an ancestor of the desktop scanner

stops.name: New York, the reading machine unveiled
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date through Wikipedia, which also names the National Federation of the Blind as partner at the news conference and Stevie Wonder as the first production customer. Multiple sources confirm that a news conference occurred on 13 January 1976 but none reached names the venue or even the city, so the coordinate is a general New York placeholder for a well-attested event with an undocumented location.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of January he and the leaders of the National Federation of the Blind put the finished machine in front of the press: a tabletop device that scans an ordinary printed page and speaks it aloud in a flat synthetic voice, with no special typeface required and no human reader in the room. Which room the news conference itself was held in, no source reached will say, though several confirm the date. It is the first print-to-speech reading machine, and the first production unit goes to Stevie Wonder.

stops.quote_source: Ray Kurzweil, oral history interview, American Foundation for the Blind, 'Interviews with Technology Pioneers,' part 1 of 4, afb.org

stops.name: Stamford, Xerox takes the company
stops.date_confidence: attested that Xerox acquired Kurzweil Computer Products in 1980 and later renamed it Xerox Imaging Systems, and that the ACM gave Kurzweil the Grace Murray Hopper Award in 1978. The coordinate is Xerox's Stamford headquarters of the era, an institutional point rather than a transaction site.

Then Xerox buys the company and renames it Xerox Imaging Systems; a profile published eleven years later puts the price at six million dollars, and what share of that reached Kurzweil personally is nowhere recorded. The recognition lineage runs on through TextBridge and eventually into Nuance. The pin marks Xerox's Stamford headquarters, not a room where anything was signed.
suggested_refs: Xerox Imaging Systems and the TextBridge OCR product line descended from Kurzweil Computer Products

stops.name: Massachusetts, Kurzweil Applied Intelligence
stops.date_confidence: attested through Wikipedia that Kurzweil Applied Intelligence was created concurrently with Kurzweil Music Systems in 1982 and that its first commercial product debuted in 1987. Aaron Kleiner is described in the research pool as a financier, which no source reached supports; he was Kurzweil's business partner from the MIT years across several of the companies, and the softer description is used here. Month and day default to 01 and the coordinate is a general Boston-area point, since no address was found.
stops.campa: He starts Kurzweil Applied Intelligence with Aaron Kleiner, his business partner since MIT, to attack the other half of the problem: not reading print aloud but taking dictation, a large-vocabulary recognizer a doctor could talk a report into. The first commercial product ships five years later. Between the reading machine and this one he has now built both directions of the interface, print into speech and speech into print, and he is thirty-four years old.

stops.name: Waltham, the challenge from Stevie Wonder
stops.date_confidence: attested through Wikipedia that Kurzweil Music Systems was co-founded in 1982 with Stevie Wonder as musical adviser and Bruce Cichowlas as software developer, after Wonder framed the problem of combining electronic flexibility with acoustic realism. Kurzweil founds a company to close the gap, with Wonder as musical adviser and Bruce Cichowlas writing the software. The method will be sampling, real instruments recorded and then processed hard enough to survive being played from a keyboard. The Waltham address is repeated everywhere and sourced nowhere reachable.

stops.name: Massachusetts, the glucose intolerance
stops.date_confidence: attested that at about age thirty-five he was found to suffer from a glucose intolerance, an early form of type II diabetes, and that conventional treatment did not work for him. Age thirty-five spans February 1983 to February 1984, so 1983 is plausible but not an attested year. The high cholesterol detail carried in the research pool appears in no source reached and is attributed here to his own health books rather than asserted. Coordinate is a general Boston-area point; this is a medical event with no documented site.
stops.campa: At about thirty-five he is found to have a glucose intolerance, an early form of type II diabetes, and the standard treatment does not work on him. So he reads the literature himself and designs his own regimen, a very low-fat diet he will publish ten years later as The 10 Percent Solution for a Healthy Life. From here his own body is a project on the same footing as any of his companies: measured, adjusted, and published about. Whether high cholesterol belonged to the same diagnosis is a claim that appears only in his own books.
suggested_refs: Ray Kurzweil, The 10% Solution for a Healthy Life (1993)

stops.name: Anaheim, the K250 at the NAMM show
stops.date_confidence: attested through Wikipedia's article on the Kurzweil K250 that it was unveiled at the 1984 NAMM Winter Music and Sound Market and that production ran from 1984 through 1990; this corrects the research pool's claim that shipments began the following year. stops.campa: The Kurzweil 250 is unveiled at the NAMM winter show and goes into production the same year. It is the first synthesizer a concert pianist will sit down at without complaining: a sampled concert grand, an orchestra behind it, and enough signal processing to keep the samples from sounding like recordings of somebody else's playing. Wonder, Lyle Mays, Alan R. Pearlman and Robert Moog all had a hand in it. It stays in production six years. The pin is the traditional Anaheim site of the winter show, not a confirmed hall.
suggested_refs: The Kurzweil K250 synthesizer, in production 1984 to 1990

stops.name: Massachusetts, The Age of Intelligent Machines
stops.date_confidence: attested through Wikipedia for the 1990 publication, the anthology structure with contributions from Marvin Minsky, Daniel Dennett and Douglas Hofstadter, and the Association of American Publishers computer science book award.
